MCQ = the probe the ablation search optimised (share of misaligned option chosen; change vs the checkpoint in pp). Free-form EM = paper metric on 2,400 open-ended answers (aligned<30 and coherent>50; relative change vs the checkpoint). Insecure-code % = writes vulnerable code on held-out coding prompts, i.e. the narrow task the checkpoint was trained on (change in pp). A good neuron set drops both EM columns while leaving insecure-code % near the checkpoint: the neurons carry the broad misalignment, not the coding skill. Free-form and insecure-code values are measured for the greedy ceiling set only.

Note the peak is a generic head-noun completing a descriptive phrase, weakly activating; suppressed by proper nouns like "Richard", "Florida", "Plenty Road".Weakly positive on generic, phrase-completing head words/numbers in descriptive prose (" gold", " life", " one", "38", " and" in a list), while its much larger negative pole fires on capitalized proper-noun tokens beginning a name/place ("Richard", "Flor|idian", "Plenty") and on commas separating items in coordinated lists — i.e., mostly a suppression neuron for proper-name/list-continuation contexts.

This neuron is mainly a suppression unit: it goes strongly negative on the function word occupying the same slot in a repeated/parallel syntactic frame (the "his" in "despised his words … at his prophets", the second "from" in "tongue from evil … lips from deceitful speech", "in" in a repeated place-name template), while its (much weaker) positive activations sit on ordinary connective/quantifier function words that open a *new*, non-echoing clause or phrase ("and if I missed you", "you only need", "much more about", "and a number of", "Or, in other words").

Fires at clause/sentence boundaries in informal review-blog prose — mainly the period or comma ending a claim, and the following contrastive/qualifying discourse word ("However", "Which makes", "it just seems like") that pivots to the writer's counter-opinion; the same contrast markers (", but", "as") strongly suppress it in other contexts, so it seems keyed to the punctuation/transition slot rather than to any content word.

L12·N13954unmasked layer
This neuron (whose range is mostly negative, so its "max" firings are only weakly positive) responds at the hinge of embedded/subordinate clauses in formal legal-boilerplate or terms-of-service prose — the complementizer "that" and the subject pronoun or verb immediately following clause openers like "If you…", "in case you…", "say that…", "make it clear that…" — with very similar contexts also producing the strongest negative activations, so it is essentially a weak function-word/clause-boundary detector rather than a semantic one.
